solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Extremely nervous cricketers approaching ton (8)

blocks.note: the Windies are the West Indies cricket team
T is the standard abbreviation for a ton

annotation.surface: A batting side, jittery as one of them nears a century.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ton' in a cricket surface wants to be a hundred runs, but here it is only the weight abbreviation T. To be windy is British slang for being scared.
annotation.definitionFit: Windy is informal British for nervous or frightened, so the windiest are the most extremely nervous.

entries.clue: Opening batting, Cook parts with wickets (6)

indicatorNotes.parts with: To part two things is to push them apart and stand between them, so IN and DO go between the two wickets.

blocks.note: W is the scorecard abbreviation for a wicket, and the plural gives two of them
the side batting is the side that is in
to do food is to cook it, as in doing the potatoes

annotation.surface: An opening batsman named Cook loses wickets at the start of an innings.
annotation.walkthrough: Alastair Cook was an England opening batsman, so 'Opening batting, Cook' reads as a cricket report; 'Opening' is really the definition and Cook a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A window is an opening in a wall to let in light.

entries.clue: Deny entry to bear regularly seen around (6)

indicatorNotes.to bear: In a down clue what bears something holds it up from below, so GATE sits underneath the other piece.
indicatorNotes.regularly: Taking letters regularly means at a steady stride, here the second and fourth.
indicatorNotes.around: Turning around puts the letters in the opposite order.

blocks.note: the even letters of sEeN, turned around
a gate is a way of entry

annotation.surface: A bear kept out of somewhere it keeps being spotted nearby.
annotation.definitionFit: To negate a claim is to deny it or declare it untrue.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bear' pretends to be the animal; here it means carry, and in a down clue the lower piece carries the upper one.

entries.clue: Domestic scenes at home, rioters upset (9)

indicatorNotes.upset: Something upset is knocked over and jumbled, so the letters of RIOTERS are rearranged.

blocks.note: someone at home is in
RIOTERS rearranged

annotation.surface: Rioters disturbed while indoors, a scene of domestic chaos.
annotation.definitionFit: Interiors are paintings of rooms inside a house, the domestic scenes of Dutch art for example.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Domestic scenes' sounds like family rows to match the rioters, but it means paintings of rooms.

entries.clue: Contrived French artist about to install magenta bust (5-7)

indicatorNotes.about: About means turned round, so the artist's name is written backwards.
indicatorNotes.to install: To install something is to put it inside, so the jumbled colour goes into the reversed name.
indicatorNotes.bust: Something bust is broken, so the letters of MAGENTA come out in a new order.

blocks.note: Edgar Degas, the painter of ballet dancers, reversed
MAGENTA rearranged, placed after the S

annotation.surface: A French painter moving a bust into place, or smashing some magenta paint.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bust' pretends to be a sculpture for the artist to install; it is the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Something stage-managed is arranged behind the scenes to look spontaneous, which is to say contrived.

entries.clue: Old flame giving up nothing for one who wanted more (6)

indicatorNotes.giving up: Giving something up means letting it go, so the O of LOVER leaves.
indicatorNotes.for: One thing for another means in exchange for it, so I takes the O's place.

blocks.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
an old flame is a former lover
nothing is zero, the letter O
one is the Roman numeral I

annotation.surface: A former sweetheart who gave up on someone always wanting more from them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old flame' reads as a single idea, but it splits in two, and the swap of nothing for one turns a sweetheart into an organ.
annotation.definitionFit: Oliver Twist is the workhouse boy in Dickens who famously asked for more gruel.
annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a clause standing for a person, 'the one who wanted more'; the setter lets 'one' serve the wordplay as I and the definition at once.

entries.clue: Whitefly in greenhouse to some extent remaining (5)

indicatorNotes.to some extent: Only part of the phrase is used, so the answer sits inside the words that come before.

blocks.note: inside whitefLY IN Greenhouse

annotation.surface: Some whitefly still hanging on in a greenhouse.
annotation.definitionFit: Something lying somewhere is staying there, as in snow lying on the ground, so it is remaining.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across three words of the surface, starting in the insect's name.

entries.clue: Plucky Dublin broadcaster cycled back, partly (8)

indicatorNotes.cycled: Letters that are cycled go round like a wheel, so the front BRA comes off and is added at the end.

blocks.note: plucky means brave
RTÉ is Ireland's national broadcaster, based in Dublin

annotation.surface: A plucky Irish broadcaster who cycled back home.
annotation.walkthrough: BRAVE and RTE give BRAVERTE; cycling its first three letters to the end gives VERTEBRA. 'Back' looks like part of the cycling instruction, but it belongs to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A vertebra is one of the bones of the spine, so it is part of the back.

entries.clue: Money deposited in bank just yesterday? (8)

indicatorNotes.deposited in: Money deposited in a bank goes inside it, so CENT goes inside RELY.

blocks.note: to bank on someone is to rely on them
a cent is a coin, a small amount of money

annotation.surface: A question of whether cash paid in only yesterday has cleared.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank' looks like a noun for the money to go into; it is the verb bank on, RELY. The question mark flags yesterday as one example of recently.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done just yesterday was done recently; the question mark marks it as an example.

entries.clue: Man unleashing tackles, essentially to shock winger (8)

indicatorNotes.unleashing: To unleash something is to let it go, so the K drops out of KNIGHT.
indicatorNotes.essentially: The essence of a word is its core, here the middle letter of tackles.

blocks.note: a knight is a chess man
the middle letter of tacKles
to jar is to jolt or shock

annotation.surface: A rugby player putting in heavy tackles to shake up the opposing winger.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Winger' and 'tackles' paint a rugby wing, but a winger is anything with wings, here a bird. 'Man' is a chess piece.
annotation.definitionFit: The nightjar is a nocturnal bird, and a winger is crossword shorthand for any bird.

entries.clue: Cold vermouth, full-flavoured but short of lemon (6)

indicatorNotes.short: Something short is cut off before its end, so RICH loses its last letter.

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
It is Italian vermouth, as in gin and it
a rich sauce is full-flavoured; short, it is RIC

annotation.surface: A chilled vermouth that is rich but has no lemon in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Short of lemon' reads as lacking a lemon twist, but 'short' trims RICH and 'of lemon' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Citric describes the acid in citrus fruit, so it means of or from lemons.

entries.clue: Funds put back into business to check kit for office? (12)

blocks.note: to rein in is to check or hold back
a vestment is a robe a cleric wears for a religious office

annotation.surface: A firm ploughing money back into itself so it can buy office supplies.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Office' suggests a workplace, but it is a church service, and the kit is the robe worn for it.
annotation.definitionFit: Reinvestment is putting profits back into a business rather than paying them out.

entries.clue: Might one find fish fresher in Billingsgate Market? (5)

indicatorNotes.in Billingsgate Market: Billingsgate is London's fish market, and its Cockney porters are known for dropping their H's, so HOTTER loses its H.

blocks.note: fresher news is hotter, just in

annotation.surface: A shopper wondering whether the fish is fresher at London's famous fish market.
annotation.walkthrough: Billingsgate is London's old fish market, famous for Cockney porters who drop their H's, so hotter is said 'otter. 'Find fish' reads as shopping, but an otter hunts them.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: otters are river hunters that live on the fish they catch.

entries.clue: Enduring evening of poetry, run into extreme bores (9)

indicatorNotes.into: Going into something means going inside it, so R sits within VERGE.
indicatorNotes.bores: To bore is to drill through, so VERGE with R pushes into the middle of E'EN.

blocks.note: e'en is the poetic contraction of even, evening
the verge is the extreme edge
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run

annotation.surface: A poetry evening that seems to go on forever because of dreadfully boring readers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bores' is not dull people but the verb drill, and 'extreme' is a noun meaning edge. E'en is the poetic contraction of even, an old word for evening.
annotation.definitionFit: Something evergreen stays fresh and popular for ever, so it is enduring.

entries.clue: I, for one, spread normal manure (5,7)

indicatorNotes.spread: Manure is spread about the field, and the letters are scattered into a new order.

blocks.note: NORMAL MANURE rearranged

annotation.surface: A gardener admitting to spreading ordinary muck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I, for one' looks like the speaker introducing themselves; it is the letter I as an example of a numeral.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the letter I stands for one in the Romans' number system.

entries.clue: Plant, contrary woman planted across ridge (9)

indicatorNotes.planted across: Something planted across something else straddles it, so MARY goes around CHINE.

blocks.note: from the nursery rhyme Mary, Mary, quite contrary
a chine is a ridge, as of a hill or a backbone

annotation.surface: A contrary gardener putting a plant in along a ridge.
annotation.walkthrough: The rhyme's Mary is a gardener, which is why the clue is full of plants; 'Plant' itself is industrial machinery.
annotation.definitionFit: Plant is the machinery and equipment used in industry.

entries.clue: Proclaim a booklet’s charms (8)

indicatorNotes.Proclaim: To proclaim words is to say them out loud, so it is their sound that counts.

blocks.note: a tract is a short booklet, often religious

annotation.surface: Someone declaring the appeal of a little pamphlet.
annotation.definitionFit: To attract someone is to charm them, and both are verbs in the third person.
annotation.walkthrough: A tract is a short pamphlet, usually religious or political, handed out to persuade.

entries.clue: Pillar of the community highlighting hit job (8)

blocks.note: to lamp someone is slang for hitting them
a post is a job

annotation.surface: A respected local figure exposed as behind a contract killing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pillar of the community' is a pillar that literally lights up the neighbourhood, and 'hit job' splits into two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A whimsical description: the post is a tall column holding a street light, a pillar that keeps the neighbourhood lit.

entries.clue: Being Frank Spencer, maybe handling spanner calamitously (12)

indicatorNotes.handling: To handle something is to hold it, so TRACY holds the jumbled spanner.
indicatorNotes.calamitously: Something done calamitously goes badly wrong, so the letters of SPANNER are thrown into disorder.

blocks.note: Spencer Tracy, the Hollywood actor, is one Spencer
SPANNER rearranged

annotation.surface: Frank Spencer, the disaster-prone hero of the British sitcom Some Mothers Do 'Ave 'Em, wrecking things with a spanner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frank Spencer' is a single name on the surface, but 'Frank' closes the definition and 'Spencer, maybe' is Spencer Tracy.
annotation.definitionFit: Transparency is openness and honesty, the quality of being frank.

entries.clue: Setter cracking grin, beaming like a Cheshire cat? (6)

indicatorNotes.cracking: To crack something is to break into it, so I goes inside SMILE.

blocks.note: a grin is a smile
the setter speaking of themself is I

annotation.surface: A crossword setter breaking into a broad Cheshire-cat grin.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark shows the definition is an example: 'like a Cheshire cat' is a comparison, which is what a simile is.
annotation.definitionFit: A simile compares one thing to another using like or as, and grinning like a Cheshire cat is a stock example.

entries.clue: Pure Charlie? It’s superior to speed (6)

indicatorNotes.It’s superior to: In a down clue what is superior sits above, so C comes on top of HASTE.

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
haste is speed

annotation.surface: Someone arguing that a person called Charlie is better than going fast.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' also reads as cocaine, and 'speed' as amphetamine, so the surface compares drugs; 'Pure' is the definition, not a drug's quality.
annotation.definitionFit: Chaste means pure, abstaining from sex.

entries.clue: Driving away, individual avoided reversing fast (9)

indicatorNotes.reversing: Reversing means going backwards, so LEPER is written back to front.

blocks.note: a leper is a person everyone shuns
Lent is the Christian fast before Easter

annotation.surface: A driver going backwards to swerve round someone at speed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fast' suggests speed in a driving clue, but it is the religious fast, LENT.
annotation.definitionFit: Something repellent drives things away, as insect repellent does.

entries.clue: City under feudal tenure (5)

blocks.note: Liège is a city in eastern Belgium
in the feudal system a vassal owed service to the lord whose land he held

annotation.surface: A town still run on medieval landholding rules.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Under' looks like a down-clue placement instruction, but it belongs to the second definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A liege man held land from his lord under feudal obligations, and Liège is also a Belgian city.

entries.clue: Race diary is periodically quiet (5)

indicatorNotes.periodically: Periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken.

blocks.note: the even letters of dIaRyIs
sh is the call for quiet

annotation.surface: A racing diary that is only kept now and then and says little.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Race' sounds like horse racing to go with the diary, but it means a people.
annotation.definitionFit: The Irish are a people or nation, which is one old sense of race.

entries.clue: Artisan wine and beer finally introduced by supermarket (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points to the end of each word, so wine and beer give their last letters.
indicatorNotes.introduced by: Something introduced by another comes after it, so CO-OP goes in front.

blocks.note: the Co-op is a British supermarket chain
the last letters of winE and beeR

annotation.surface: A craft wine and beer range being launched by a supermarket.
annotation.walkthrough: The Co-op is a British supermarket chain. 'Artisan' pretends to describe the drinks, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A cooper is a craftsman who makes barrels, so an artisan, fittingly one who holds wine and beer.

entries.clue: Contradictory beliefs present opposing views lacking focus (8)

indicatorNotes.lacking focus: The focus of a word is its centre, so SIDES loses its middle letter D.

blocks.note: someone present is here
the two sides of an argument

annotation.surface: A debate laying out opposing viewpoints that never get to the point.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Contradictory' means contradicting accepted doctrine, not self-contradicting.
annotation.definitionFit: Heresies are beliefs that contradict orthodox teaching.

entries.clue: Faced with series of games, support Chesterfield? (6)

blocks.note: a set is a series of games in tennis
a tee supports a golf ball

annotation.surface: A question about backing Chesterfield football club through a run of fixtures.
annotation.walkthrough: Chesterfield is an English football club, which fits the games, but a chesterfield is also a padded leather sofa.
annotation.definitionFit: A chesterfield is a kind of sofa, so an example of a settee; the question mark signals the example.

entries.clue: Component of plastic heel, new yet needing repair (8)

indicatorNotes.needing repair: Something needing repair is broken, so the letters are rearranged.

blocks.note: used as it stands
N is the abbreviation for new
used as it stands

annotation.surface: A shoe with a plastic heel that has broken though it is brand new.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is shoe repair; 'plastic' belongs to the definition, not the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Ethylene is the gas polymerised to make polythene, so it is a component of plastic.
